title: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
subject: Medicine
summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency. Diagnosis relies on hyperglycaemia and low C‑peptide. Management centres on lifelong insulin replacement and monitoring for acute and chronic complications.

sections.p: An autoimmune disease where >80% of beta cells are destroyed, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Diagnosis requires documented hyperglycaemia plus evidence of beta‑cell failure.
b: Random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with classic symptoms
Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L on two occasions
2‑hour OGTT glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L
Low or undetectable C‑peptide in the presence of hyperglycaemia

t.b: Does the patient meet the hyperglycaemia threshold? ≥11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes in symptomatic patients.
Is there endogenous insulin production? Low/undetectable C‑peptide supports type 1 over type 2.
Do autoantibodies confirm autoimmune aetiology? Positive result strengthens type 1 diagnosis, especially in atypical age.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by glycaemic control (HbA1c) and presence of acute complications (DKA, hypoglycaemia). No formal staging system, but clinicians use risk categories.
b: HbA1c <7 % – good control
HbA1c 7–9 % – moderate control
HbA1c >9 % – poor control, high complication risk

t.b: What is the average glucose over 2–3 months? Guides intensity of insulin regimen and predicts microvascular risk.
Is the patient in ketoacidosis? Positive ketones with acidosis indicate DKA, an emergency.

sections.p: Autoimmune destruction is primary; in low‑resource settings, viral infections (e.g., enterovirus), malnutrition, and certain medications can precipitate or unmask the disease.
b: Autoimmune beta‑cell attack (GAD65, IA‑2 antibodies)
Enteroviral infection (coxsackie B) – common trigger in Africa
Iatrogenic beta‑cell loss (e.g., chronic streptozotocin exposure)
Concurrent HIV infection – may accelerate beta‑cell loss

sections.p: Classic triad of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss; in children, may present with DKA. In low‑resource settings, presentation is often delayed, with severe dehydration and altered mental status.
b: Polyuria with nocturia
Polydipsia, dry mouth
Unexplained weight loss despite normal intake
Fatigue, blurred vision
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath

sections.p: Focus on confirming diagnosis, assessing control, and detecting complications. When a test is unavailable, use clinical proxies.

t.b: Is the patient hyperglycaemic now? Guides immediate insulin dosing.

t.a: Urine dipstick for glucose and ketones
t.b: Is there glucosuria and ketonuria? Supports diagnosis and flags DKA risk.

t.a: Serum electrolytes and arterial blood gas
t.b: Is there metabolic acidosis with anion‑gap elevation? Confirms DKA.
What is long‑term control? Fructosamine reflects 2‑3 weeks of glucose.
Are there early diabetic retinopathy changes? Detects microvascular disease.

sections.p: Acute: DKA, severe hypoglycaemia. Chronic: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease. In low‑resource hospitals, infection and delayed presentation increase mortality.
b: DKA: vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, altered consciousness
Severe hypoglycaemia: seizures, loss of consciousness
Progressive visual loss – possible retinopathy
Proteinuria – early nephropathy
Peripheral neuropathy – burning feet, loss of sensation

sections.p: Insulin replacement is mandatory; regimen chosen to match lifestyle and resource availability. Education, monitoring, and treatment of emergencies are essential.
b: Basal‑bolus insulin (long‑acting + rapid‑acting) – mimics physiologic secretion
Premixed insulin (70/30) – useful where multiple daily injections are difficult
Avoid sulfonylureas – they require endogenous insulin
Treat DKA with IV regular insulin, fluids, and electrolyte correction
Educate on sick‑day rules and hypoglycaemia recognition

sections.p: Regular review every 3 months for HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, and foot exam. Prevent complications with tight control, vaccination, and lifestyle advice.
b: HbA1c every 3 months; target <7 %
Blood pressure <130/80 mmHg
Annual retinal screening
Urine microalbumin annually
Foot inspection at each visit

sections.p: Conditions that share polyuria/polydipsia or hyperglycaemia.
b: Type 2 diabetes – differs by insulin resistance and preserved C‑peptide early
Diabetes insipidus – polyuria/polydipsia without hyperglycaemia
Hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state – occurs in type 2, no significant ketosis

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal early in disease or altered by co‑existing conditions.
b: C‑peptide may be detectable early in the honeymoon phase, misleading toward type 2
Urine glucose can be negative if renal threshold is high (e.g., chronic kidney disease)
HbA1c may be falsely low in anaemia or recent blood loss

whenToSeekHelp: Altered mental status, seizures or coma – possible DKA or severe hypoglycaemia
Persistent vomiting with dehydration – risk of DKA progression
Chest pain or dyspnoea – possible cardiac ischemia in poorly controlled diabetes

faq.a: It reflects endogenous insulin production; low levels confirm absolute insulin deficiency.

faq.q: Can type 1 diabetes present in adulthood?
faq.a: Yes, latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA) is a slower‑progressing form but still requires insulin.
A temporary period after diagnosis when residual beta‑cells produce some insulin, lowering insulin needs.

exam: A 12‑year‑old presents with polyuria, weight loss and a random glucose of 13 mmol/L – what are the next two investigations and why? — Check C‑peptide to confirm insulin deficiency and autoantibodies to support autoimmune aetiology.

A patient with known type 1 diabetes arrives unconscious, breathes deeply and smells of acetone – what is your immediate management? — Recognise DKA; start IV fluids, give regular insulin infusion, monitor electrolytes and treat acidosis.
Why is a sulfonylurea contraindicated in type 1 diabetes? — It stimulates endogenous insulin which these patients lack, offering no benefit and risking hypoglycaemia.

How would you differentiate type 1 diabetes from diabetes insipidus in a low‑resource setting? — Measure plasma glucose; hyperglycaemia points to diabetes mellitus, normal glucose with dilute urine suggests diabetes insipidus.

A pregnant woman with type 1 diabetes has an HbA1c of 8 % – what target should you aim for and why? — Aim for <6.5 % to reduce fetal macrosomia and congenital anomalies, balancing maternal hypoglycaemia risk.

What are the key components of sick‑day rules for a child with type 1 diabetes? — Continue basal insulin, check glucose every 4 h, treat >15 mmol/L with correction dose, treat <4 mmol/L with rapid carbohydrate, seek care if ketones appear.
Explain why retinopathy screening should start 5 years after diagnosis in children. — Microvascular damage accumulates over time; early detection allows laser treatment before vision loss.
In a patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, how might type 1 diabetes presentation differ? — HIV can accelerate beta‑cell loss and mask symptoms; drug interactions may affect insulin absorption.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and physical exam identify classic type 1 diabetes features, rule out mimics, and detect acute complications such as DKA or severe hypoglycaemia.
b: Onset: rapid (weeks‑months) vs gradual; ask age at first symptoms.
Polyuria: frequency, nocturia, any change after fluid restriction.
Polydipsia: volume, preference for sweet drinks, effect on weight.
Weight loss: amount, intentional vs involuntary, associated appetite changes.
Fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infections.
History of autoimmune disease (thyroiditis, celiac), family history of type 1 diabetes, HLA‑related relatives.
Recent viral illness (enterovirus, coxsackie), malnutrition, HIV status, TB exposure, pregnancy.
Medication review: steroids, antiretrovirals, herbal remedies that affect glucose.
Previous episodes of DKA or severe hypoglycaemia, sick‑day management knowledge.

t.b: Look for dehydration (dry mucosa, reduced skin turgor), weight loss, breath odor; positive indicates volume depletion but cannot quantify fluid loss.
Check heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory pattern (Kussmaul); tachypnoea suggests metabolic acidosis, but does not give pH.
Tenderness, guarding may indicate DKA‑related ileus; percussion for tympany; cannot diagnose ketoacidosis without labs.
Assess mental status, focal deficits; altered consciousness points to severe DKA or hypoglycaemia, but does not differentiate cause.
Assess perfusion; absent pulses suggest severe dehydration, but cannot quantify electrolyte disturbances.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and point‑of‑care tests answer diagnostic, severity, and complication questions; alternatives are provided for low‑resource settings.
b: Random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with classic symptoms confirms diabetes.
Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L on two occasions confirms diabetes.
2‑hour OGTT glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes.
C‑peptide low/undetectable with hyperglycaemia confirms absolute insulin deficiency.
Autoantibodies (GAD65, IA‑2, ZnT8) confirm autoimmune aetiology.
HbA1c reflects average control over 2‑3 months; <7 % good, 7‑9 % moderate, >9 % poor.
Serum ketones or β‑hydroxybutyrate ≥0.6 mmol/L indicates ketosis; >3 mmol/L suggests DKA.
Arterial blood gas: pH <7.3, bicarbonate ≤15 mmol/L confirms DKA severity.
Electrolytes: Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ guide replacement; K⁺ <3.3 mmol/L requires replacement before insulin.

t.b: Diagnoses diabetes when ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms; if lab unavailable, use glucometer reading.
Diagnoses diabetes when ≥7.0 mmol/L on two separate days; if fasting not possible, use random glucose with symptoms.
Assesses chronic control; <7 % good, 7‑9 % moderate, >9 % poor; if unavailable, use average of three fasting glucose values.
Distinguishes absolute from relative insulin deficiency; low/undetectable confirms type 1; if assay unavailable, rely on autoantibodies and clinical picture.
Confirm autoimmune etiology; positive supports type 1; if not available, diagnosis rests on clinical features and C‑peptide.
Quantifies ketosis; ≥0.6 mmol/L indicates ketosis, ≥3 mmol/L suggests DKA; if unavailable, use urine ketone dipstick (semi‑quantitative).
Determines acid‑base status; pH <7.3, HCO₃⁻ ≤15 mmol/L defines DKA; if ABG unavailable, use venous blood gas with correction.
Guide fluid and insulin therapy; hyperkalaemia common in DKA, but total body K⁺ low; replace K⁺ when >3.3 mmol/L before insulin.
Screening tool for ketosis; dark purple indicates high ketones; cannot differentiate β‑hydroxybutyrate from acetoacetate.

sections.p: Classification combines biochemical thresholds, clinical presentation, and complication burden to guide management intensity.
b: Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes: any of the glucose criteria plus evidence of absolute insulin deficiency (low C‑peptide or positive autoantibodies).
Staging (ADA/International Society): Stage 1 – autoimmunity positive, normoglycaemia; Stage 2 – dysglycaemia, no symptoms; Stage 3 – clinical diabetes with symptoms.

t.b: Autoantibodies present, normal glucose; monitor every 3‑6 months, no insulin needed yet.
Abnormal OGTT or HbA1c 5.7‑6.4 % with autoantibodies; intensified monitoring, consider enrolment in prevention trials.
Symptomatic hyperglycaemia, glucose criteria met, insulin required; severity stratified by HbA1c and presence of DKA.

t.a: Severity grading (based on HbA1c and acute state)
t.b: Good control: HbA1c <7 %; moderate: 7‑9 %; poor: >9 % or current DKA; guides frequency of follow‑up and education intensity.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic type 1 diabetes; careful history, targeted bedside tests, and selective investigations separate them, especially where resources are limited.
b: Diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic) – polyuria/polydipsia without hyperglycaemia.
Type 2 diabetes in young people – often obesity, insulin resistance, C‑peptide preserved.
Maturity‑onset diabetes of the young (MODY) – autosomal dominant, mild hyperglycaemia, preserved C‑peptide.
Cushing’s syndrome – hyperglycaemia with characteristic stigmata, cortisol excess.

t.b: Key point: urine osmolarity low (<300 mOsm/kg) despite high serum osmolarity; water deprivation test distinguishes central vs nephrogenic; glucose normal, so bedside glucose test rules out diabetes mellitus.
Usually overweight, acanthosis nigricans, C‑peptide normal/high; autoantibodies negative; fasting insulin elevated; bedside BMI and skin exam help differentiate.
Family history of early‑onset diabetes, mild hyperglycaemia, preserved C‑peptide, negative autoantibodies; genetic testing definitive but not required for initial management.
Features: centripetal obesity, striae, hypertension; random glucose may be elevated; overnight dexamethasone suppression test confirms; bedside signs point away from pure autoimmune diabetes.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides acute stabilization, transition to basal‑bolus insulin, ongoing monitoring and timely referral.
b: 1. Confirm DKA or severe hypoglycaemia; start IV fluids (0.9% saline) and correct electrolytes before insulin.
2. Initiate rapid‑acting insulin infusion (e.g., regular insulin) after potassium ≥3.3 mmol/L; target glucose drop 5–10 mmol/L per hour.
3. Switch to subcutaneous basal‑bolus regimen once acidosis resolves and patient can eat: long‑acting insulin (e.g., glargine) + rapid‑acting before meals.
4. Educate on carbohydrate counting, sick‑day rules and glucose self‑monitoring; set target fasting 4–7 mmol/L, post‑prandial <10 mmol/L.
5. Escalate to specialist diabetes team if recurrent DKA, HbA1c >9 %, or psychosocial barriers; refer to ophthalmology after 5 years or at puberty, whichever is later.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Insulin therapy carries predictable adverse effects; recognising them early prevents morbidity.
b: Weight gain: counsel on balanced diet and regular activity; adjust basal dose if excess persists.
Lipodystrophy at injection sites: rotate sites each dose; avoid repeated use of same area.
Allergic reaction to insulin (rare): switch to a different insulin analogue or use an antihistamine; avoid if anaphylaxis.

t.b: Avoid – adds hypoglycaemia risk without benefit in absolute insulin deficiency.
Expect increased insulin requirements; increase basal dose proportionally.
Mask hypoglycaemia symptoms; monitor glucose more frequently.

sections.p: Identify acute and chronic threats; thresholds trigger specialist input.
b: Recurrent DKA (≥2 episodes/year) – refer to tertiary diabetes centre for intensive education and possible pump therapy.
Persistent HbA1c >9 % despite adherence – consider psychosocial review, insulin regimen optimisation, or continuous glucose monitoring.
Severe hypoglycaemia requiring third‑party assistance – assess for insulin dosing errors, consider basal dose reduction.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, test interpretation and therapy.
b: HIV infection: may accelerate beta‑cell loss; antiretrovirals (e.g., protease inhibitors) increase insulin resistance – raise insulin dose.
Tuberculosis: rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, lowering insulin levels – monitor glucose closely during treatment.
Severe malnutrition: reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis; risk of hypoglycaemia – use lower insulin doses and frequent glucose checks.
Pregnancy: insulin requirements rise 1.5‑2‑fold; avoid oral agents; target fasting <5 mmol/L, post‑prandial <7 mmol/L.
Alcohol binge: inhibits gluconeogenesis, precipitating hypoglycaemia – advise moderate intake and monitor after drinking.

t.b: Insulin clearance falls; reduce total daily dose by 20‑30 % and avoid rapid‑acting bolus stacking.
Impaired insulin degradation; monitor for hypoglycaemia and adjust doses accordingly.
May potentiate insulin effect; ask patients to disclose use and watch for low glucose.

sections.p: Tailor management to physiological and resource constraints of each population.
b: Children: use weight‑based basal‑bolus; involve caregivers in carbohydrate counting; screen for growth delay; start retinopathy screening after 5 years or at puberty.
Pregnancy: switch to rapid‑acting and long‑acting analogues with proven safety; increase monitoring frequency to every 1‑2 weeks.
Elderly: start with low‑dose basal insulin; avoid hypoglycaemia by targeting higher glucose (7–10 mmol/L); consider cognitive status before pump use.
People with HIV: coordinate with ART clinic; monitor for drug‑induced insulin resistance; screen for opportunistic infections that may affect glucose.
Low‑resource settings: use premixed insulin if analogues unavailable; rely on urine glucose strips when glucometers fail; prioritize education on sick‑day rules and hydration.

t.b: Ask about polyuria, nocturia, weight loss, recent infections, and family history of autoimmunity.
Inspect for dehydration, weight loss, acanthosis nigricans (rare in type 1), and check for ketotic breath; palpate abdomen for tenderness indicating DKA.
Use urine ketone dipstick and capillary glucose; if ketones + glucose >13 mmol/L with dehydration, treat as presumptive DKA.

facts: Random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with classic symptoms confirms diagnosis
Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L on two separate days confirms diagnosis
Low or undetectable C‑peptide in hyperglycaemia indicates absolute insulin deficiency
HLA‑DR3‑DQ2 and HLA‑DR4‑DQ8 are the highest‑risk HLA combinations
GAD65, IA‑2 and ZnT8 antibodies are the three routine auto‑antibodies
Enterovirus (coxsackie B) infection is a common environmental trigger in Africa

vivas.q: What is the first cellular event after insulin binds its receptor on a target cell?
vivas.a: Autophosphorylation of the β‑subunit of the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase.

vivas.q: Which auto‑antibody is most sensitive for early detection of β‑cell autoimmunity?
vivas.a: GAD65 antibodies, detectable months before hyperglycaemia.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate type 1 diabetes from diabetes insipidus in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Measure urine specific gravity; dilute urine (<1.005) suggests DI, whereas concentrated urine (>1.020) with hyperglycaemia suggests type 1 diabetes.

vivas.q: Why are sulfonylureas contraindicated in type 1 diabetes?
vivas.a: They stimulate endogenous insulin release, which is absent due to β‑cell destruction, providing no glucose‑lowering effect and risking hypoglycaemia if residual β‑cells are minimal.

vivas.q: What bedside test can confirm ketosis in a child with suspected DKA?
vivas.a: Positive urine dipstick for ketones (acetone) using nitroprusside; confirms ketonaemia when clinical picture fits DKA.

vivas.q: What is the primary metabolic shift that drives acetoacetate and β‑hydroxybutyrate production in DKA?
vivas.a: Increased hepatic fatty‑acid β‑oxidation with diversion of acetyl‑CoA to ketogenesis due to insulin deficiency and excess glucagon.

vivas.q: List the three auto‑antibodies used to detect β‑cell autoimmunity and a brief clinical relevance for each.
vivas.a: GAD65 – earliest marker; IA‑2 – high specificity; ZnT8 – adds sensitivity in seronegative cases.

vivas.q: Describe the four stages of the natural history of type 1 diabetes.
vivas.a: Stage 1: autoimmunity, normoglycaemia; Stage 2: autoimmunity, dysglycaemia; Stage 3: clinical diabetes; Stage 4: long‑term complications.

vivas.q: Explain the genetic susceptibility to type 1 diabetes beyond HLA alleles.
vivas.a: Non‑HLA genes such as INS VNTR, PTPN22, and IL2RA modestly increase risk and interact with environmental triggers.

vivas.q: How does concurrent HIV infection alter presentation of type 1 diabetes?
vivas.a: HIV may accelerate β‑cell loss, cause atypical hyperglycaemia, and antiretroviral drugs (e.g., protease inhibitors) can worsen insulin resistance.

vivas.q: What are the key components of sick‑day rules for a child with type 1 diabetes?
vivas.a: Frequent glucose monitoring, adjust insulin for illness, maintain hydration, treat ketones promptly, and seek medical care if vomiting persists.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line insulin regimen for a newly diagnosed child with type 1 diabetes?
vivas.a: Multiple daily injections: basal long‑acting insulin plus rapid‑acting bolus before meals.

vivas.q: Why is a high anion‑gap metabolic acidosis a hallmark of DKA?
vivas.a: Accumulation of keto‑acids (β‑hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) adds unmeasured anions, raising the anion gap.

vivas.q: What bedside sign suggests dehydration in DKA?
vivas.a: Dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor; orthostatic hypotension if severe.

vivas.q: How does malnutrition affect insulin requirements in type 1 diabetes?
vivas.a: Reduced caloric intake lowers insulin dose; risk of hypoglycaemia increases, requiring careful dose adjustment.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a low C‑peptide level in a hyperglycaemic patient?
vivas.a: Confirms absolute insulin deficiency, supporting a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes rather than type 2.

mcqs.q: A 14‑year‑old presents with polyuria, weight loss and a random glucose of 13 mmol/L. Which additional finding most strongly supports type 1 diabetes over type 2?
mcqs.e: Autoantibodies are specific for autoimmune β‑cell destruction.

mcqs.q: In DKA, which metabolic pathway is up‑regulated, leading to ketone production?
mcqs.e: Insulin deficiency drives hepatic fatty‑acid oxidation and ketogenesis.

mcqs.q: After an insulin bolus, which intracellular event occurs first in muscle cells?
mcqs.e: Insulin signaling rapidly causes GLUT4 vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane.

mcqs.q: Glucose uptake into adipose tissue under insulin stimulation primarily uses which transport mechanism?
mcqs.e: Insulin‑dependent GLUT4 mediates glucose entry into adipocytes.

mcqs.q: Which HLA genotype confers the highest risk for type 1 diabetes?
mcqs.e: The DR4‑DQ8 combination is strongly associated with disease susceptibility.

mcqs.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with severe dehydration, fruity breath and Kussmaul respirations. Which shift explains the high serum acetone?
mcqs.e: Insulin deficiency promotes lipolysis, providing substrate for hepatic ketone production.

cases.v: A 12‑year‑old boy from a rural clinic presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and occasional vomiting. Random capillary glucose is 14 mmol/L. Urine dipstick is positive for ketones. No prior medical history.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management step?
qs.a: Diabetic ketoacidosis; start IV isotonic saline, then insulin infusion after confirming potassium.

qs.q: Which bedside test helps confirm ketosis?
qs.a: Positive urine nitroprusside dipstick for acetone; if unavailable, check breath for fruity odor.

qs.q: What long‑term education should be given to the family?
qs.a: Insulin administration basics, glucose monitoring, sick‑day rules, and importance of regular follow‑up.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman (28 weeks) with known type 1 diabetes reports a HbA1c of 8 %. She feels well and has no hypoglycaemic episodes.

qs.q: What HbA1c target is appropriate in pregnancy and why?
qs.a: Aim for ≤6 % to reduce risk of macrosomia, pre‑eclampsia and congenital anomalies, while avoiding hypoglycaemia.

qs.q: Which insulin regimen is preferred in pregnancy?
qs.a: Multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion using rapid‑acting and basal analogues, avoiding oral agents.

qs.q: How often should fetal growth be monitored in this scenario?
qs.a: Serial ultrasound every 4 weeks, with additional scans if glycaemic control is suboptimal.

mistakes: Confusing HLA‑DR3/DR4 as a single risk allele; the risk lies in specific DR‑DQ haplotypes (DR3‑DQ2, DR4‑DQ8).
Stating retinopathy screening begins ‘5 years after diagnosis or at puberty, whichever is later’; guidelines require screening after 5 years of disease regardless of puberty timing.
Listing sulfonylureas as a treatment option for type 1 diabetes; they are ineffective and can cause hypoglycaemia.
Assuming a normal C‑peptide rules out type 1 diabetes; residual C‑peptide may persist early in disease.
Relying solely on fasting glucose to diagnose DKA; ketone measurement and acid‑base status are essential.
Prescribing metformin in a child with type 1 diabetes; it is not first‑line and lacks evidence in absolute insulin deficiency.
